newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-AUSTRALIA TRANSPORT - OPINION - Transport Workers' Union.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-AUSTRALIA TRANSPORT - OPINION - Transport Workers' Union.

text.p: By John Allan (Federal Secretary of Transport Workers Union)
FREEDOM OF ASSOCIATION
The Transport Workers' Union (TWU) has achieved something in the order of 51 percent unionisation in the private transport industry.

A large part of those who remain un-unionised are in areas where the TWU does not have a history of organising, or where structural and legal impediments make organising more difficult, most particularly;
- employees in the long distance sector
- employees and owner drivers in taxi and courier sectors
- owner-drivers of trucks (particularly linehaul)
- non-driver employees (particularly clerical employees)
- employees in provincial centres, or in the hinterland
DEMOCRATS HAVE FAILED TO UNDERMINE WORKPLACE RELATIONS ACT

The Workplace Relations Act embodies a fundamental change in industrial relations. The amendments sought by the Australian Democrats do not, in any way, undermine the fundamental workings of the Act, nor do they attempt to challenge the assumptions which underpin the Act.
The Australian Democrats posture that they have shielded workers from the full impact of the Act. In fact, they have accepted;
- the Coalition drive to break up collective bargaining and replace it with individual employment contracts;
- the erosion of Federal Awards, in both the coverage of those awards and the notion of "allowable matters";
- that individual employment agreements are secret and, largely, not scrutinised by the Commission;

- that unions and their roles be contained and attacked by new "tame cat" enterprise unions, a diminution in right of entry to stifle union growth and re-growth, secondary boycotts to weaken union industrial power, and facilitate the deamalgamation and break-up of existing unions.

Further, the Democrats have gone so far as to endorse and co-sponsor the Act. Thus the political atmospherics of the Act are very positive for the government, in that, it appears to have compromised and won the support of an "honest" and "non-partisan" political party that aims to "keep the bastards honest".
The betrayal of the Democrats is indicative of the fact that they are not industrial relations practitioners, nor do they have an industrial focused constituency;
- they are susceptible to a small business and small "L" Liberal constituency which is attracted to the government's lip-service notions like "individual choice" and "freedom of association";
- they are intending to give away here so as to expand their political capital on the Telstra debate.
Thus the Workplace Relations Act is the child of idealogies within the Liberal party, and the Democrats have willingly served as mid-wives through a combination of naivete and political expediency.

This does not augur well for those of us who are practitioners within the present day industrial relations regime, and who ultimately bear responsibility for the outcomes served up to both the organisations that drive the system, and the broader community who wear the results.
WILL ENTERPRISE UNIONS EMERGE?

Where the union movement has made mistakes, or has little or no presence, and where the employers are canny and anti-union, enterprise unions may emerge. However, I suspect that they will not be either widespread phenomena.
The CRA's of this world may foment the creation of an enterprise union as a means of foiling genuine union organisation, or perhaps to assist in avoiding federal award coverage.

The promotion of enterprise unions is nothing more than a mechanism whereby employers can construct compliant unions. Enterprise unions by their very nature, will not be in a position to deploy either significant resources, an industry-wide perspective nor industrial relations expertise in their endeavours.
Enterprise unions are a means to divide unions, divide workers, and sap the collective resources and industry-wide strength of unions.
RIGHTS OF ENTRY

By attacking a union's right of entry, the government seeks to cripple union organisation and the promotion of unionism amongst non-union workers. Thus, it represents a fundamental attack on the grass roots of union organisation.

The new provisions will enable officials to enter workplaces where the union has membership, or where there are persons eligible to be members of a particular union, so that discussion can be held in non-working times.
To investigate a breach the official may require the employer to produce documentation within usual office hours.
The official must always give the employer 24 hours notice prior to exercising any right.
In practice, where a union has existing membership, a sound workplace structure of delegates and the like, and where the union is seen to be relevant and strong, these provisions will have no effect.

Where unions seek to expand in the non-union sector, these rules do start to impinge upon unions. Also it is important to note, right of entry does not apply to employees on individual employment contracts, or Australian Workplace Agreements (AWAs).

Officials may not see any documentation that relates to AWAs - their secrecy is protected at every stage. This provides a further incentive to militant employers to engage in the making of individual employment contracts - union officials' right of entry does not apply.
(The views expressed are John Allan's own and do not represent the views of Reuters.)
